problem: The answer claims the processor-time product matches the serial arithmetic cost. It does not: with O(n²) processors and about n log n parallel steps, processor-time product is O(n³ log n), which is a factor log n above the serial O(n³). So the algorithm is not work-optimal in the standard sense; only its flop count equals the serial one.
fix: Q5 answer: The flop count is O(n³), the same as serial elimination, so no arithmetic is wasted — every element update is useful work. But the parallel time is about n log n (broadcast included), so the processor-time product is O(n³ log n) and speedup is near n/log n. It is work-optimal only if you count arithmetic operations and ignore the log n broadcast cost; textbooks therefore call it not work-optimal.

where: Section 2, sentence starting 'With O(n²) processors the arithmetic work is O(n³)'
problem: The term 'work-optimal in arithmetic' is not a standard term and can mislead, because work is normally parallel time × processors, which here is O(n³ log n), so the algorithm is not work-optimal.
fix: Write: 'With O(n²) processors the flop count is O(n³), the same as serial elimination. Counting only arithmetic, no work is wasted; but the total work including the log n broadcast per column is O(n³ log n), so the method is not work-optimal.'

problem: The question asks for the Jacobi update in words, but the answer only repeats the formula.
fix: Answer in words first: 'Take the old guess x_old, keep only the diagonal part on the left, move the off-diagonal contribution (L+U)x_old to the right, and divide each equation by its diagonal entry.' Then add: x_new = D⁻¹(b − (L+U)x_old), one matrix-vector product per sweep, so every component is independent and the sweep is data-parallel.
